metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
The structural weight capacity of data center floors has become a limiting factor in AI deployment, often constraining retrofits before electrical capacity does.

Data centers built for previous generations of servers were designed around lighter, air-cooled equipment. Liquid cooling systems add significant weight through coolant, manifolds, and supporting infrastructure. Modern AI racks, particularly those optimized for dense compute, exceed the load ratings that raised floors and concrete slabs were engineered to support. A building with ample electrical supply and sufficient space can still be unable to host the hardware its power infrastructure could feed.

This constraint matters because it extends the timeline of AI scaling beyond what power planning alone suggests. A facility cannot simply upgrade its electrical service and immediately achieve higher utilization. Structural retrofitting, when possible, requires expensive reinforcement. Many existing data center sites hit this structural ceiling before they approach their electrical limits, forcing operators to either abandon buildings or pursue slower, more costly repairs than adding capacity elsewhere.

The metric does not reveal how many facilities face this limit, how often it blocks deployment relative to other constraints, or whether new construction can fully avoid it given the rapid acceleration of rack density and weight.
